title: How ventilation therapy supports breathing
intro: Ventilation therapy uses a machine to help a person breathe when the lungs or breathing muscles cannot do the job well enough on their own. It can be used for a short time during illness or surgery, or over months and years at home for long-term conditions. Understanding the main types helps patients and families take part in decisions about it.

sections.heading: Why breathing support is needed
paragraphs: Breathing depends on healthy lungs, strong breathing muscles and a brain that controls the rhythm of breaths. When one of these fails, the body may not take in enough oxygen or may not get rid of enough carbon dioxide. This can cause breathlessness, tiredness, headaches, confusion or morning drowsiness.

Conditions that may lead to ventilation therapy include severe pneumonia, advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, neuromuscular diseases, severe obesity with breathing problems and some injuries or operations. The cause and the expected course of the illness strongly influence which approach is chosen.

sections.heading: Non-invasive ventilation
paragraphs: Non-invasive ventilation delivers air under gentle pressure through a tight-fitting mask over the nose or over the nose and mouth. The device helps the lungs expand and eases the work of the breathing muscles. It is often used at night, sometimes also for several hours during the day.

Many people at home use this form of treatment, for example with chronic lung disease or muscle weakness. A good fit matters: the mask should seal without causing pressure sores, and the pressure settings are adjusted by a specialist team. Dry mouth, skin irritation and a feeling of air pressure are common early complaints that can often be improved.

sections.heading: Invasive ventilation
paragraphs: Invasive ventilation uses a tube placed through the mouth or nose into the windpipe, or through a small opening in the neck called a tracheostomy. The machine then delivers the breaths. This is usually done in an intensive care unit, where patients are given medicines for comfort and are closely monitored.

Doctors aim to use it for as short a time as the illness allows. Possible complications include lung infections, lung injury from pressure and muscle weakness after a long stay, which is why rehabilitation is an important part of recovery.

sections.heading: Living with home ventilation
paragraphs: People using ventilation at home and their relatives are trained to use and clean the equipment, handle alarms and know what to do if power fails. Regular check-ups assess how well the treatment works, often with blood tests of oxygen and carbon dioxide or overnight measurements.

Practical topics include travelling with the device, speech and swallowing, nutrition, and arranging help at home. Support from specialised nurses, respiratory therapists and patient groups can make daily life easier.

sections.heading: Making decisions together
paragraphs: Ventilation can improve symptoms and sometimes extend life, but it also brings burdens. Questions about goals, comfort and what the person would want should be discussed early, ideally while the person can still take part. Advance care planning documents can record these wishes.
If a person cannot speak for themselves, trusted relatives or a legal representative may be asked to help interpret the person's wishes together with the medical team.

examples.title: Getting used to a mask
examples.text: Imagine you have just started overnight mask ventilation and find the mask uncomfortable. You could note when it leaks or hurts, then ask the team to refit it, try another size or adjust the humidifier rather than simply stopping the treatment.

examples.title: Planning ahead with family
examples.text: Suppose a close relative has a progressive muscle disease and may later need ventilation. The family could arrange a calm conversation with the doctors about what the relative values most, what treatment burdens are acceptable, and how those wishes will be written down.
